repo_notes.content: WHAT THIS FILE IS, AND THE ONE RULE THAT GOVERNS EVERY NOTE IN IT. This is a standing instruction set for generating the wiki, not a description of the repository. It is written once and read on every generation, against a codebase that moves — so a sentence here that states the repository's CURRENT STATE is a sentence that will be wrong on some future run, with nothing to notice. Counts, inventories, prop lists, config values, dependency versions, file sizes, class names and route lists therefore DO NOT BELONG HERE. They belong in the repository, where they are true by construction, and they are to be derived at generation time. This is not a hypothetical: an earlier revision of this file told a generator the site's total client JavaScript was two inline scripts when the build shipped three, and located the offset plate in a shortcut it had been factored out of — both read as confident, settled fact, and both were instructions to write something false. WHEN THIS FILE AND THE CODE DISAGREE, THE CODE WINS, including against sentences here that sound certain; say so in the generated page rather than reproducing the wrong side. What earns a place here is only what a generator cannot get by reading: who the wiki is for, what to generate and what to leave out, how to derive each class of fact, the traps that make a careful reading come out wrong anyway, and where the non-derivable knowledge is written down.

AUDIENCE AND VOICE. This wiki serves two readers, in this order: (1) the maintainer returning after months away, who needs invariants, gotchas, why-decisions and where-to-change-what, fast; (2) recruiters and peer engineers evaluating the engineering practice. Always prefer explaining WHY a decision was made and WHAT BREAKS if it is violated — and naming the test or comment that guards it — over restating what the code does. The 'what' is a small number of short .astro files that anyone can read in minutes; the 'why' is the part that took work and the part that is not in the code. Write in the present tense about the present state, and attribute every quantitative claim to the file it came from.

THE PRIMARY SOURCES ARE IN THE REPOSITORY, AND THEY ARE THE WHY-COMMENTS. This codebase carries an unusual amount of measured rationale in comments — the workflow headers, the theme-token block in the layout, uno.config.ts, the grid comment in the home page, the JSDoc in src/lib/, and the doc block at the top of each file under tests/. Quote them with line anchors rather than paraphrasing: they are dense and they carry the measurements, and a paraphrase keeps the conclusion while dropping the evidence, which is the half worth reading. When one of them contradicts a note in this file, quote the comment. Several of those comments also record their OWN earlier drafts being wrong, and say so in place — that is a house style, not an accident, and it is worth showing the reader an example of it rather than describing it.

HOW TO DERIVE, BY DOMAIN — the replacement for every fact this file used to state. Routes and pages: enumerate src/pages/ and the built HTML; note that one rest-parameter route can build several pages, so count the output, not the source files. Client-side JavaScript: enumerate the script elements in the built pages and the ones authored under src/ — the site's identity is having no external JS FILES, which is not the same as having no JS, and the difference has been got wrong here before, so state both and derive both. CSS: ask what a PAGE loads through the helper in tests/helpers/ rather than by reading the built asset directory, because inlining and chunk-splitting both make the directory a wrong answer. Icons: read the safelist in uno.config.ts together with the mapping helper in src/lib/, and note what the safelist deliberately does not cover and why the comment says so. Styling vocabulary: read the shortcuts out of uno.config.ts, name each one and say what wears it, deriving the wearers from the components. Content: read the exports of the modules under src/content/ and src/data/; some of them reach no card on any page, so check each one's consumers rather than assuming it is rendered. Tests: enumerate the suites and take each one's subject from its own doc block. Deploy: read .github/workflows/. Plan status: read the execution table in plans/README.md. In every one of these, if a figure is needed, derive it and anchor it to the file and lines it came from; if a figure is not needed, do not introduce one.

ABSENCE IS USUALLY A RECORDED DECISION HERE, AND MUST NEVER BE WRITTEN UP AS A GAP, A BUG OR A TODO. This repository has an unusually strong habit of recording what it decided NOT to do, together with the evidence that killed it: plans/README.md has sections for findings considered and rejected, for work deliberately not planned, and for open items that are the maintainer's call and not an agent's, and individual absences carry a why-comment at the place where the thing is missing. So when something looks obviously missing — a dependency that appears unused, a lint glob that seems too narrow, a browser test that seems overdue, a header that is not set, a record that is not managed, a field that is configured and never rendered — go and look for the note before writing a word about it, and present what you find as a decision with its reasoning. Two standing prohibitions come out of that habit and are policy rather than fact: never tell a reader to make a change in a vendor dashboard when the thing is managed as code in this repository, and never propose a gating check that runs against a deployed preview URL, which cannot be ordered because the URL does not exist until the deploy it would gate has already happened.

UPSTREAM CONTAMINATION IS THIS REPOSITORY'S CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE MODE FOR GENERATED DOCS. It began as a fork of Ladvace/astro-bento-portfolio and has diverged substantially since, and earlier auto-generated documentation blended upstream features and pre-refactor code into descriptions of this repository — component props that never existed here, client-side behaviour that was deleted, libraries that were removed. The pattern is that the invented detail is PLAUSIBLE, which is exactly why it survives review. So: re-derive every claim about a component's props, its slots and anything it does at runtime from the current source, and treat a recollection that sounds right as a reason to check rather than a reason to write. The deletions are also this repository's whole identity and worth documenting AS deletions — read them out of the plans ledger, in the past tense, and never let one appear in the present.

MEASUREMENT TRAPS WORTH CARRYING, because they are about how to read evidence and stay true as the code changes. A status code is not an answer to 'can a reader see this' — fetch the page and read it; the repository records a case where a 200 with no redirect was recorded as proof a page was public and the page said 'log in to see this'. Name the edge and the grid: a sweep that measured one edge does not license a claim about a class, and several comments here record a conclusion that was inverted because of exactly that. Say which instrument produced which number — arithmetic over authored colours and a probe of composited pixels answer different questions, and a comment here was corrected for attributing one to the other. A probe can report a feature it cannot actually set, so a guard can look tested when nothing was tested. A behavioural probe cannot see a redundancy that something upstream is masking. And a check that reads sensibly can still evaluate false on a payload where the object it references is absent, which is why the workflow guards are EXECUTED rather than read. When a page in this wiki quotes a measurement, quote the instrument with it.

SCOPE, AND WHAT NOT TO GENERATE. Ignore build output, dependency directories, scratch directories, and the lockfile. README.md owns getting-started and setup — link to it, never write a second setup guide, and treat the repository's own contributing and operational documents the same way, since one of them may already own whatever a page here is tempted to explain. CLAUDE.md is instructions to a coding agent, not subject matter for a human wiki. Generated endpoints under src/pages/ that emit text files are to be described by their DERIVATION, never by their emitted text, and no page is to be built out of that text. This is a small site, so generate exactly the pages specified below: no page per component, no glossary, no contributing guide, no roadmap, no FAQ. The infrastructure directories are in scope but belong inside the deploy page rather than getting pages of their own. Package management is pnpm; the manifest pins it.

plans/ IS A DECISION LEDGER, NOT SOURCE CODE, AND IT HAS ITS OWN READING ORDER. plans/README.md is the living index and its execution table is the authoritative status source — its own prose header has demonstrably lagged its own table, so read statuses from the table. Never present a plan that has not shipped as shipped, and never describe the pre-change architecture in an archived plan as current: those files are frozen by design and go on naming what they deleted, which is what makes them a record. plans/done/ carries the per-plan verification evidence — what was mutation-tested, what each preview-versus-production diff showed, what defects were found during execution — and is where to go for why something was done a particular way. Take the next plan number from the index; numbering is monotonic across runs.

pages.title: Overview: The Site, and What Was Removed to Get It
pages.purpose: Orient both audiences in one read. Say what the site is — a personal portfolio built on Astro and UnoCSS, statically generated, deployed to Cloudflare Pages by GitHub Actions — and derive the route list and the shape of each route from the repository rather than restating one. Frame the engineering identity as SUBTRACTION, and lead with the thesis that gives the identity teeth: each removal is locked rather than merely done, by an assertion in the suite rather than by a sentence in a document. Build the headline story as a compact before/after table, taking each row from the plans ledger with its plan number and its completion commit: what the output used to be and what it is now, what the client runtime used to be and what replaced it, how icons used to be delivered and how they are now, and what now stands between a red suite and a deploy. Be precise about the strongest claim on this page: the site ships no external JavaScript FILE, which is a claim about the build output and is directly asserted by name in the build-output suite — quote the test names literally. It is NOT a claim that no JavaScript runs, and the two have been conflated here before; enumerate what does run, from the build, and say which pages carry which. Include one system diagram: the content and data modules, the components that consume them, the prerendered output, the suites that assert against that output, the uploaded artifact, and the host. Note the fork lineage. Close with a documentation map, DERIVED rather than recited: list the Markdown documents the repository actually carries at its root and beside the directories they describe, and take each one's subject from its own opening lines rather than from a remembered division of labour. That division has moved — material has been relocated out of the front-page README into documents beside the code it describes — so any map written here would be a map of the arrangement on the day it was written. Add one line saying which of the wiki's own pages is the first stop after time away.

page_notes.content: This is the recruiter landing page: keep it short and diagram-led. Anything removed appears only in the 'before' column with a plans citation, never in the present tense. Completion commits and plan numbers are history and do not rot, so they are safe to quote — unlike anything describing current state, which must be derived. 'Maintainer Playbook' and 'Engineering Log' are sibling pages of this wiki, not files in the repository.

pages.title: Maintainer Playbook: Invariants and Change Recipes
pages.purpose: The page the maintainer opens after six months away. Structure it as task-oriented recipes, each naming the exact file to edit, the trap that fires if the edit is incomplete, and a link to the system page that explains the mechanism. Derive the recipe list from what the repository actually makes editable — read the exports of the content and data modules and ask, for each, what else moves when it moves. The recipes that matter are the ones where ONE edit is not enough, so hunt for those specifically: a value that several surfaces derive from, a hand-maintained list that must be extended in lockstep with a generated one, a grid that is packed exactly full so that adding a card requires re-balancing others, an icon that renders as nothing unless a safelist also learns about it, and a width or height budget that a longer string can overrun. Each of those has a comment or a test naming the failure; quote it. Include the iteration shortcut for the suite, taken from the test setup file. Then a hard 'do not helpfully fix this' section, built by reading the rejected-findings and deliberately-not-planned sections of the plans index rather than from memory — for each entry give the one-line reason and the link to the evidence, and present it as a decision.

page_notes.content: Recipes deliberately restate invariants that the system pages own, but as one-line trap plus link, not as full mechanism. Verify every file reference against current source at generation time, and derive which surfaces a value feeds rather than listing them from a previous generation — that list has grown every time the site did.

pages.title: Architecture: Layout, Routes, and Component Contracts
pages.purpose: Document the render path and the component contracts. Start from the shared layout, which wraps every page and builds the whole document head from the content modules — social and card metadata, the canonical link, a structured-data block, the analytics tag, and the inline scripts. Enumerate the client scripts from two sources — every script authored under src/ and every script present in the built HTML — and treat those as different questions, because the layout's scripts ship on every page while a component's ship only onto the pages that use that component; say which pages carry which. Distinguish first-party from third-party, and inline from external file: the site's identity claim is about external FILES, not about whether any JavaScript runs, and those two have been conflated here before. Derive each script's purpose from the comment above it rather than from its code, and expect the purposes to share a shape — each exists because something has to happen either side of the moment the page can style itself: the theme has to resolve before first paint or the reader sees a flash, and a press has to outlive the finger, because the finger lifts long before the navigation happens. NEVER STATE OR IMPLY THAT THE SCRIPTS YOU FOUND ARE ALL THERE ARE. An earlier revision of this file enumerated only the layout's scripts and called them the site's entire client runtime, which was wrong — it is the same error this file's opening note records, re-committed inside the rewrite meant to remove it, and it survived because a closed set written in English is still a count. That is why the enumeration is instructed here rather than answered. For any script whose job is to hold a state across a navigation, describe what it REFUSES as carefully as what it does — each refusal is a way of stranding a control on a page that never leaves — and note that its declarations are authored as twins of the ones the press already had, so the site behaves identically with the script absent. Then the routes: derive them from src/pages/, and be specific about which route builds several pages and about the page that exists to answer a URL the site does not have, including why a static host makes that page necessary and what the layout prop it uses turns off. Then the grid: read the home page's own comment for the packing arithmetic and quote it verbatim, because it changes whenever the cards do. Explain the height budget as a FLOOR WITH NO CEILING and the row sizing as content-driven, and give the accessibility criterion that requires both — a reader may enlarge type without moving any font-size the page can see, so a grid that cannot grow deletes the difference. Give a compact component roster derived from the components directory, not subpages, and for each one state its contract: the props and slots it actually declares, and any accessibility contract it carries. Cover the icon and screen-reader conventions as RULES rather than as inventories — when an icon is decorative, when it needs a companion for a screen reader, when a link that opens a new tab says so — and derive the wearers of each rule from the source, since every one of those sets has grown at least once.

page_notes.content: Verify every prop, slot and accessibility claim against current source. This repository's own pre-refactor components had props that no longer exist and client-side behaviour that was deleted, and prior generated docs described both as present — so a plausible-sounding contract is a reason to open the file. Where an earlier revision of this wiki asserted a count of the elements wearing a convention, that count was wrong within one release; derive it or omit it.

pages.title: Content as Typed Data
pages.purpose: Explain the repository's core pattern: user-facing copy and authored data live as typed, test-gated modules under src/content/ and src/data/, with a suite as their validator rather than a linter. Derive each module's subject from its own head — they say what they hold, and how the material is divided between them has been reorganised once already, so read the heads rather than assuming the division. Walk the exports, derived at generation time, and for each say who consumes it. Give particular attention to the ones whose consumer is not a card on a page, because they read as dead code and are not: some are rendered only into a generated text endpoint, some belong to a single route, and at least one is configured, deliberately unrendered and one edit from returning, with a comment saying so. Explain the icon indirection: icons are stored as Iconify identifiers and converted to utility classes by one helper, which both the components and the build config's safelist must go through, and an identifier that the safelist never learns about produces correct markup, a green build and nothing on screen. Note that the safelist deliberately does not cover every collection of icon-bearing data and read the config's comment for why. THE TRAP ON THIS PAGE: src/content/ is a name Astro reserves for content collections, and the modules in it are ordinary source only while the repository has no collection config — check whether that is still so, and read the repository's own note on it, before describing them as collections, because the obvious reading is the wrong one. The page's story is the gating decision: these modules sit outside the lint glob on purpose and the suite is the validator instead — cover what that suite checks, including the drift gate that requires the site's own meta description to name each goal's target figure, which exists because a description drifted from the goals it described and shipped. Diagram the flow from the modules into the components, forking into the in-process render that one suite asserts and the built output that another does. Derive which exports each suite actually asserts from its imports rather than assuming full coverage — a coverage gap existed here once and was closed by a plan. Close with the static assets the site references and where each is used.

page_notes.content: Read the export list, the goal figures and every numeric bound off the modules at generation time. Never freeze a kilometre figure, a length bound, a count of exports or a count of modules into prose: the figures are bot-updated daily, the export list has grown every release, and the modules themselves have been split apart once already. An earlier revision of this file enumerated the exports by hand and had lost three of them, and named a single module that no longer exists.

pages.title: Styling, Theming, and the Icon Pipeline
pages.purpose: Document the coupled UnoCSS systems whose failure modes are SILENT — that is the through-line, and every section should name the silence. Icons are CSS mask rules generated from Iconify data, so the site ships no inline SVG and no icon font; the coupling to the safelist is the first silent failure, and the preset's extra properties are the second — read them out of the config and explain what each one prevents, since without them an icon is present in the markup and invisible on screen, at the wrong size or in the wrong place relative to the text baseline. The config records measured alternatives for those values; quote the measurement rather than the number alone. Next, the control vocabulary: read the shortcuts out of the config, name each one, say what it is FOR and derive what wears it from the components — this set has grown from one to several and a previous revision of this file sent readers to the wrong member of it. State the rules that govern the set rather than its membership: a control declares its box rather than capping it, and whether it pins or floors that box follows from whether its label comes from data; the geometry suite discovers controls from a signature in the shipped stylesheet rather than from a list, so a new variant is caught rather than skipped. Then the two interaction rules, both of which are enforced build-wide with no carve-outs: a hover style must need a pointer to produce it, which a preset achieves by rewriting every hover utility into a pointer-gated rule and which depends on that preset's ORDER in the presets array — below the base preset it silently emits nothing and looks exactly like a working config; and a press must be drawn and must outlive the finger, which pairs a pressed state with an attribute-driven twin and forbids the transition that would make a short tap show a fraction of the ink. Say why the twin is an attribute and never a class, in terms of what the orphan gate reads. Theming: colour is CSS custom properties scoped to a theme attribute on the root, not framework theme tokens; read the token block's header comment, which defines each token's ROLE and states the polarity rule for the progress bar and the convention for a token chosen against one surface and used on another. Walk the flash-free flow from the pre-paint script through to the toggle. Finally the motion inventory, derived from the stylesheets: name each animation, say what triggers it, and state which ones have a reduced-motion opt-out and which do not — report an ungated one plainly rather than papering over it. Close with the second silent-failure class: a mistyped utility generates nothing, with no warning, so enumerate the reintroduction gates in the build-output suite that make that loud.

page_notes.content: This page owns the icon-safelist, control-vocabulary and animation invariants; the playbook links here. Anchor every claim to lines in the build config, the layout, the components it describes, or the build-output suite. Read the shortcut names, the token names and the animation list at generation time — all three have changed, and each time a hand-written list here went stale silently.

pages.title: Test Harness: A Green Build Is Not Evidence
pages.purpose: The strongest showcase page. Frame it with the principle stated in the build-output suite's own doc block: assert on rendered HTML and on real build artifacts, never on exit codes. Enumerate the suites at generation time and give each one the question it uniquely answers, taken from its own doc block rather than invented — one renders a page in-process through Astro's container API and asserts the content reaches it, one gates the data module, one opens the real build output, several hold geometry and layout properties that a stylesheet alone cannot express, some read the workflow files and EXECUTE their conditions in GitHub's own expression evaluator rather than reading them, and one has the repository's own documentation as its subject and asserts the prose against the code. Pick out the assertions that are unusual and say why each exists: the one that decodes actual pixels because the framework silently drops an image candidate that would upscale and only pixels catch it; the ones whose calibration is recorded in a comment because the obvious version of the assertion stayed green against the very change it existed to catch; and the ones that discover their subject from the shipped output instead of from a list, so that a new case joins the gate by existing. That last property is the page's real argument, so give it a section: a hand-kept list is the failure mode, and several gates here were rewritten to discover rather than enumerate. Surface the mutation-testing habit that the comments record — an assertion is only trusted here after someone broke the thing it guards and watched it go red — and quote a couple of the recorded cases where that came out surprising. Cover the harness mechanics a returning maintainer needs: the global setup that builds once, the environment variable that reuses an existing build, why the setup clears stale output from a deleted adapter first, and the parser quirk that decides how assertions on built pages have to be written. Quote in-file comments verbatim rather than paraphrasing.

page_notes.content: Do not hardcode a suite count, a file count or an assertion count — read them from the suites at generation time, and prefer naming what each suite proves over saying how many things it proves. Real test names and in-file comments quoted with line links are better documentation than any paraphrase, and they are the credibility anchor for the recruiter audience.

pages.title: Deploy Pipeline: Actions Builds It, the Host Serves It
pages.purpose: Explain the pipeline that ships the site and be exact about what ORDERS it. Read the workflows and derive the job graph: which job builds and gates, which jobs deploy, what each deploy job publishes, and what event each one answers. The safety property is the dependency edge from deploy to build, and the page should say plainly why it is fragile in a way a platform build command was not — on a host whose build command WAS the suite, 'a red suite cannot deploy' was a property of the platform, and here it is one edge in a job graph that a refactor can drop while every check stays green. That is why a suite reads these workflows and executes their conditions against a table of event payloads: a condition that reads sensibly can still evaluate false where the object it references is absent, and a skipped job renders as a grey check that reads like a pass. That defect shipped once. Cover the deliberate asymmetries a reader would otherwise try to fix, deriving each from the workflow and quoting the comment that explains it — most of them turn on a single question, which is whether a value ships publicly, and on the principle that nothing holding a deploy credential should also run repository source. Explain any freshness gate the deploy jobs carry and what re-running a failed job would otherwise republish. Then the other workflows: derive them from the workflows directory and give each its trigger, what it changes, and how it relates to the site build — including any that deliberately does not gate the site and is instead gated by its own review. For infrastructure managed as code in this repository, explain the plan-then-apply split, the credential split that makes it real rather than procedural, and what the scheduled run is FOR — the point is that drift between the repository and the live system surfaces as a red check rather than as a discovery. Describe records or resources deliberately left unmanaged as EXCLUSIONS WITH REASONS, never as gaps, and read the reasons from beside the exclusions. Cover local gates — the pre-commit hook, the lint configuration and the type-check's reach. Own the crawler surface: how the sitemap is produced, why it carries no per-URL date, and how the text endpoints derive their content. Close with the parity property that static output with no adapter buys: the local preview serves the same artifact production does.

page_notes.content: Never recommend a second CI system, a build step inside a deploy job, or a gating check that runs against a deployed preview URL — the last cannot be ordered, because the URL does not exist until the deploy it would gate has already happened. Every blocking check belongs in the build job, against the artifact; anything needing a live URL is reporting, not gating. Never tell a reader to change managed infrastructure in a vendor dashboard, and never describe a manual, checksum-carrying apply as automatic. A previous host appears in the repository's history and in archived plans: the only correct tense for it is the past.

pages.title: Engineering Log: The Decision Ledger
pages.purpose: The single history page, so that every other page describes only current state. Summarise plans/ as the repository's decision ledger and as a working example of governed agentic maintenance. This page must stay evergreen: derive the plan list, the per-plan statuses and the completion commits from the execution table in plans/README.md at generation time, and derive the run grouping from the dated headings and each plan's own planning date rather than from any count written here. Structure it in two halves of equal weight. First, the arc: group the shipped work by run and say what each milestone bought, reading the milestones out of the table rather than from a remembered list, and never presenting the list as exhaustive. Second — and this is the differentiator — the GOVERNANCE MECHANICS, which are standing policy rather than history: findings are killed by an adversarial pass and recorded WITH the refuting evidence precisely so no future run re-derives them; a section records the maintainer's explicit calls, which are decisions and not oversights; the baseline is re-verified at the start of each run, because the recorded lesson is that failures came from a plan believing something about the repository that had stopped being true; and the bar for calling a plan done is mutation-tested assertions plus a diff of the preview against production. Quote that recorded lesson exactly. Present all of it as decisions, never as defects or as work waiting for the reader.

page_notes.content: Statuses, completion commits, the run grouping and the next plan number are all volatile — read every one of them from the index at generation time. Never cap the narrative at a fixed number of runs, never present a plan that has not shipped as shipped, and never describe pre-change architecture from an archived plan as current. Items recorded as resolved in the index keep their resolution: report the decision and its outcome, not the original finding.
